blocks.text: Chapter 5.
Zoom Out, Zoom In — Then Ooch
Fifth night, friend — and it opens with the world's greatest expert on human bias... walking straight into one.

Daniel Kahneman — yes, the Nobel laureate from our Thinking Fast and Slow shelf — was leading a team designing a decision-making curriculum for Israeli high schools. After a productive first year, he polled the team: how long will the whole project take? The estimates clustered around two years. Then he turned to Seymour, the team's curriculum expert, and asked a subtly different question: how have comparable teams fared?

Pause and guess: Seymour knew the track record of teams exactly like theirs. His answer stunned the room — and then the room did something even more remarkable with it. What did he say, and what did the team do?
Ready? Here is what happened.

"Roughly 40 percent of such teams never finish at all... and none finished in under seven years." And this team, he added, was if anything below average in resources. The room heard the numbers... shrugged... and kept working to the two-year plan. The curriculum took eight years, friend — and by then, nobody wanted it. That's the whole lesson in one meeting: the inside view — your plans, your talent, your special circumstances — feels rich and relevant precisely because it's built from vivid detail, and that vividness is what makes it seductive and unreliable. The outside view — the cold track record of everyone who tried what you're trying — encodes information your story cannot see. Every restaurant founder knows most new restaurants fail; almost every one believes theirs is the exception. The move is humility by arithmetic: before deciding, ask — of people who faced this same choice, what fraction succeeded, how long did it take, what did it cost? You may still proceed — sometimes the odds are worth it — but with eyes open instead of inside a flattering story. And when you consult experts, ask the right question, friend: they're terrible at predicting your specific outcome and excellent at reporting the distribution — never "will I win my lawsuit?" but "what percentage of cases like mine settle, and in what range?" Interrogate the past and the population — never your future.
Fifty thousand miles in a minivan

The outside view sets expectations — but averages hide texture, friend. So complement the zoom-out with a close-up: go see reality firsthand. Toyota institutionalized it as genchi genbutsu — go and see for yourself. Before redesigning the Sienna minivan, engineer Yuji Yokoya drove one more than 50,000 miles — all fifty states, Canada, Mexico. No spreadsheet would have told him what the road did: prairie crosswinds demanded better handling, and North American families practically live in their vans — kids' comfort and cargo flexibility mattered enormously. The redesigned Sienna's sales jumped about 60%. Franklin Roosevelt ran the same play on a whole nation: distrusting the filtered reports that reach every leader, he solicited letters from ordinary citizens — thousands a day — and had staff prepare systematic "mail briefs" of a representative sample, spot-checking batches himself. A permanent close-up no aide could distort.

The template at its most humbling came from Brian Zikmund-Fisher — a decision-theory doctoral student diagnosed in his twenties with a blood disorder that would kill him in five or six years. A bone-marrow transplant offered cure... with roughly a one-in-four chance of dying from the procedure itself. He zoomed out: survival statistics for patients like him, center by center — learning high-volume hospitals had meaningfully better outcomes. Then he zoomed in: long talks with nurses — who see the unvarnished daily reality — and with patients who'd lived through it. Statistics set the odds; close-ups revealed what the odds felt like. He chose the transplant at a high-volume center, survived, and celebrated "re-birthdays" with the daughter born after his recovery. Neither lens alone suffices, friend: the outside view can miss what makes your case genuinely different; the close-up alone is a sample of one that seduces you back into anecdote. Zoom out first, zoom in second — and when both lenses agree, move with confidence.
Why forecast when you can test?

Sometimes you can skip prediction entirely. Ooching: run a small, cheap, fast experiment and let reality answer the question you were about to answer with speculation. An Intuit team in India suspected poor farmers were underpaid because they couldn't compare prices across markets — and instead of building a product on the hypothesis, they tested it: manually texting price data to about a hundred farmers while faking the technology behind the curtain. Farmers acted, earned more — and Fasal grew to serve hundreds of thousands. Founder Scott Cook's warning deserves the wall, friend: without experiments, decisions get made by "politics, persuasion, and PowerPoint." Careers ooch too: before three years and six figures of law school — shadow a lawyer for a week. The daily reality of a job is usually nothing like the fantasy, and the test-drive costs a fraction of the wrong commitment.

Pause and guess: Hiring is where ooching most embarrasses prediction. In 1979, the University of Texas medical school admitted 150 students ranked TOP by its interviews — then the legislature abruptly expanded the class by 50, forcing the school to accept applicants from near the BOTTOM of its rankings, students virtually every school had rejected. Researchers tracked both groups for years. What did they find?
Ready? Here is what happened.

No difference. None — not in attrition, not in academics, not in clinical performance through residency. The interviews had measured essentially nothing, friend — yet interviewers walk away supremely confident, a bias Richard Nisbett named the interview illusion. Decades of research agree: interviews are among the weakest predictors of job performance — beaten by work samples, job-knowledge tests, and peer ratings of past work. The fix: assign a small paid work sample — a real task from the actual job — and weight it far above interview charm. But hear the boundary the Heaths insist on, friend: ooching is the wrong tool for decisions that require commitment to succeed. You cannot ooch your way into having a child — and half-hearted trials of all-in ventures generate misleading data, because the tentative version isn't the real thing. Worse, ooching can become socially acceptable stalling: if the analysis is done and only the leap remains, another "small experiment" isn't prudence. It's procrastination wearing a lab coat. Ooch when a cheap test can supply missing information. Commit when the information is in and only courage is missing.
Before you go

So: the master of biases watched his own team ignore Seymour's 40%; base rates beat your inside story, and experts should be asked about populations, never predictions; Yokoya's fifty thousand miles and FDR's mail sacks show what close-ups catch that summaries strip; ooch before you leap — text the farmers, hire three firms for phase one, shadow the lawyer; and when Texas admitted its interview rejects, nothing changed. This week, friend: before your next big estimate, write the base rate down first — then see how far your inside story dares to stray from it.

But even with the odds known and the tests run, friend, one saboteur remains between you and the right call: the feeling of this exact moment — the fear, the excitement, the dread of awkwardness — all shouting louder than they deserve. Tomorrow: the ten-minute, ten-month, ten-year telescope; the question that dissolves agony instantly — "what would you tell your best friend to do?" — and the quiet power of knowing your core priorities before the crisis asks. Next time: attain distance.
Key takeaways
Inside view seduces with vivid detail; the outside view — the track record of everyone who tried — carries the information your story can't see.
Kahneman's team heard "40% never finish, none under seven years"... and kept planning for two. It took eight.
Ask experts for base rates and distributions of past cases — never predictions about your specific future.
Zoom in after zooming out: genchi genbutsu — Yokoya's 50,000 miles, FDR's mail, nurses over brochures — texture the averages hide.
Ooch: small cheap tests beat forecasts — fake the backend, hire three firms for phase one, shadow the job for a week.
Interviews measure almost nothing (Texas's natural experiment); use paid work samples — but never ooch a decision that needs full commitment.
